question: A research agent on the Agent SDK sometimes spawns subagents that spawn further subagents, and a single prompt has cost over $40. The team wants a hard ceiling on spend and on how deep delegation can go. Which two settings are the MOST reliable way to enforce this? (Choose two.)
explanation: Combine the spend cap with the depth cap: max_budget_usd is compared against total cost including subagent requests, refuses new spawns at the limit, and ends the query with the budget error subtype, while the spawn-depth environment variable bounds nesting (default three layers below the main agent). Prompt wording, max_tokens, and a one-turn limit do not bound the tree.
realWorldUsage: Budget for dollars, depth for structure; the prompt is a suggestion.

options.text: Set max_budget_usd on the query so the run ends with error_max_budget_usd once total_cost_usd, including subagent spend, reaches the cap.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH through the env option to limit how many layers of subagents can nest.
Add "Do not spawn more than two subagents" to the system prompt.
options.why: The prompt only steers; the docs say to set the limits as well, because Claude Code enforces them however Claude decides to delegate.

options.text: Set max_tokens to a small value on the main query.
options.why: max_tokens caps a single response's output; it counts neither subagent requests nor nesting depth.

options.text: Set max_turns=1 so the main agent cannot call the Agent tool.
options.why: One tool-use turn can still contain Agent calls, and the ceiling would also block the ordinary tool use the task needs.

source.quote: You can cap that growth in three ways: how deeply subagents nest, how many run at once, and how much the whole query spends.

question: A long Agent SDK session stops following a "never touch the migrations folder" rule that was given in the first prompt, and the team also wants the full pre-summary transcript kept for audit. Logs show a compact_boundary message shortly before the rule was violated. Which two changes are MOST effective? (Choose two.)
explanation: Persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md because compaction replaces older messages with a summary and early instructions may not survive, while CLAUDE.md is re-injected on every request; the PreCompact hook fires before compaction (with a trigger field of manual or auto) and is the documented place to archive the full transcript. Reminders, prompt pleas, and disabling compaction do not address either need.
realWorldUsage: If a rule must outlive the conversation, it is not a message; it is configuration.

options.text: Move the rule into CLAUDE.md loaded through settingSources, since CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request.
Register a PreCompact hook that archives the full transcript before the summary replaces it.
Repeat the rule in the prompt every ten turns.
options.why: Periodic reminders still live in history that compaction can summarize away, and they add tokens to every request.

options.text: Disable compaction for the session.
options.why: Without compaction the session eventually exhausts the context window and fails; the docs treat compaction as the mechanism that keeps long sessions alive.

options.text: Add "preserve all rules" to the initial prompt.
options.why: Text in the initial prompt is exactly what compaction may summarize; asking it to preserve itself does not change where it lives.

source.quote: Persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md (loaded via settingSources) rather than in the initial prompt, because CLAUDE.md content is re-injected on every request.

question: A developer creates a Managed Agents coordinator whose multiagent roster references a "research-lead" agent, and the create request fails validation. The research-lead agent was itself defined with a multiagent roster listing two worker agents. What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: Managed Agents multiagent orchestration supports a single level of delegation: a roster entry that has its own multiagent.agents roster is rejected with a validation error. Flatten the hierarchy so the top-level coordinator references the workers directly. Roster size (up to 20 unique agents), the optional self entry, and version pinning are not the failure here.
realWorldUsage: In Managed Agents the org chart is one manager and its reports, not a tree.

options.text: Coordinators can delegate only one level deep; referencing an agent that has its own roster fails the create or update request.
The roster exceeded the maximum number of agents.
options.why: The limit is 20 unique agents per roster and this roster references one agent; count is not the issue.

options.text: The roster is missing a self entry.
options.why: The self entry is optional; it only permits the coordinator to spawn copies of itself.

options.text: The referenced agent must be pinned to an explicit version.
options.why: Without a version the reference is pinned to the latest version at coordinator creation; an unpinned reference is not rejected.

source.quote: The coordinator can only delegate to one level of agents; referencing an agent that has its own multiagent.agents roster fails the create or update request with a validation error. A maximum of 20 unique agents can be listed in multiagent.agents, but the coordinator can call multiple copies of each agent.

question: An Agent SDK service auto-approves Read, Grep, and Bash(npm test *) through allowed_tools for speed. Compliance requires that every tool invocation, including those auto-approved ones, be checked against a per-tenant policy before it runs. Where is the MOST secure place to put that check?
explanation: A PreToolUse hook is the only step that runs before every other permission step on every matching call and whose deny holds regardless of allow rules or mode; omitting the matcher makes it fire for all tools. The approval callback is skipped for auto-approved tools, PostToolUse is too late, and CLAUDE.md is advisory.
realWorldUsage: Unconditional policy goes in the hook that runs before the decision, not the callback that runs after it.

options.text: In a PreToolUse hook with no matcher, returning permissionDecision "deny" when the policy fails.
In the canUseTool callback.
options.why: Auto-approved tools never reach canUseTool; calls resolved by allow rules or the permission mode skip the callback entirely.

options.text: In a PostToolUse hook that logs violations.
options.why: PostToolUse fires after the tool already ran; it can annotate the result but cannot prevent the action.

options.text: In the tenant's CLAUDE.md as a rule the model must follow.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is instruction text, not an enforcement point; the model can fail to apply it and auto-approval executes the call anyway.

source.quote: To gate every tool call regardless of mode and rules, use a PreToolUse hook instead.

question: An Agent SDK session analyzed an authentication module and proposed a JWT design. The developer wants to explore an OAuth2 alternative using the same analysis while keeping the JWT thread intact to continue later. Which session option is the MOST appropriate?
explanation: Fork the session: forking creates a new session that begins with a copy of the original's history and diverges from that point, leaving the original's ID and history untouched so both can be resumed separately. Plain resume or continue would extend the original thread, and re-pasting loses the rest of the context.
realWorldUsage: Fork when you want two futures from one past.

options.text: Resume the session with fork_session=True so a new session starts from a copy of the history and the original is unchanged.
Resume the session by ID and ask for OAuth2 in the same thread.
options.why: Resuming appends to the original history, so the JWT thread now carries the OAuth2 detour and is no longer intact.

options.text: Start a new session and paste the JWT analysis into the prompt.
options.why: Pasting copies text, not the files read and decisions made; it rebuilds by hand the context a fork carries automatically.

options.text: Use continue_conversation=True.
options.why: Continue picks up the most recent session in the directory and adds to it, which is the very thread the developer wants to preserve.

source.quote: Fork is different: it creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original’s history. The original stays unchanged.

question: A team is about to move an autonomous agent with write access to production systems out of the prototype stage. Which two practices does Anthropic's guidance on effective agents identify as MOST important before shipping? (Choose two.)
explanation: Sandboxed testing with guardrails, and explicit stopping conditions with human checkpoints, are the two safeguards Anthropic pairs with agent autonomy, because agents carry higher cost and the potential for compounding errors. Removing checkpoints, maximizing tools, or trusting self-termination each remove a control instead of adding one.
realWorldUsage: Autonomy is granted per capability, verified in a sandbox, and bounded by a counter.

options.text: Test extensively in sandboxed environments with appropriate guardrails around the agent's actions.
Add stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations, and checkpoints where the agent pauses for human feedback.
Remove human checkpoints so the agent finishes tasks faster.
options.why: Anthropic's guidance keeps human feedback at checkpoints and blockers; removing them increases the chance of compounding errors on systems the agent can write to.

options.text: Give the agent every available tool so it never gets stuck.
options.why: A bloated tool set widens the surface for wrong actions and contradicts the guidance to keep tool sets minimal and clear.

options.text: Rely on the model to decide on its own when the task is finished.
options.why: Agents usually do terminate on completion, but the guidance explicitly adds stopping conditions to maintain control because autonomy brings higher cost and compounding error.

source.quote: The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors. We recommend extensive testing in sandboxed environments, along with the appropriate guardrails.

question: A pull-request review agent must run three independent checks on every PR: style, security, and test coverage. Each check reads many files and takes several minutes. Which Agent SDK design completes the review with the LEAST latency?
explanation: Spawn three specialized subagents in parallel: the Agent SDK documentation states that multiple subagents can run concurrently so independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum, and each keeps its file reads out of the main context. Sequential, merged, or chained designs serialize the work.
realWorldUsage: Independent checks are a fan-out, not a queue.

options.text: Define three subagents and let them run concurrently so the review finishes in the time of the slowest check.
Run the three checks in sequence in the main agent's context.
options.why: Sequential execution takes the sum of the three durations and floods the main context with every file each check read.

options.text: Combine all three checks into one subagent that uses a model with a larger context window.
options.why: One subagent still performs the checks one after another; window size does not create parallelism.

options.text: Chain the checks so each starts from the previous check's summary.
options.why: The checks are independent; chaining adds a serial dependency and latency with no benefit.

source.quote: Parallelization: multiple subagents can run concurrently, so independent subtasks finish in the time of the slowest one rather than the sum of all of them.

question: A RAG service sends a 9,000-token system prompt to Claude Sonnet 5 every 30 seconds with a single cache_control breakpoint on its last system block. usage.cache_creation_input_tokens is about 9,000 on every request and cache_read_input_tokens is always 0. The first line of the system prompt reads "Request received at 2026-09-21T09:14:07Z". What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: The per-request timestamp inside the cached prefix changes the hash every time, so the system writes a fresh entry and never reads one; move the timestamp after the breakpoint or out of the system prompt. Length, TTL and breakpoint billing all fail to explain a 9,000-token write on every 30-second request.
realWorldUsage: Grep your prompt builder for datetime calls and request IDs before you touch TTLs or model choice.

options.text: The timestamp changes the cumulative prefix hash on every request, so each request writes a new entry and never matches an earlier one.
The prompt is below the model's minimum cacheable length, so caching is skipped silently.
options.why: A 9,000-token prompt is far above the Sonnet 5 minimum of 1,024 tokens, and a below-minimum prompt would show zero cache writes, not a 9,000-token write each time.

options.text: The 5-minute TTL expires between requests, so each request has to rewrite the entry.
options.why: Requests arrive every 30 seconds and every cache use refreshes the lifetime, so expiry cannot explain a miss on every call; this is the right mechanism applied to the wrong interval.

options.text: Each breakpoint is billed as a write, so a breakpoint on every request always shows creation tokens.
options.why: Breakpoints are free; writes happen only when the prefix is new. Removing the breakpoint would remove caching entirely rather than fix the miss.

source.quote: Cache writes happen only at the breakpoint, and if that block changes (timestamps, per-request context, the incoming message), the prefix hash never matches.

question: A billing dashboard sums usage.output_tokens from every message_delta event in a stream and reports about three times the tokens the API bills. Which explanation is MOST accurate?
explanation: The token counts in each message_delta usage object are cumulative; take the value from the final message_delta instead of adding events together.
realWorldUsage: Treat streaming usage as a snapshot to overwrite, not an increment to accumulate.

options.text: The usage in message_delta events is cumulative, so the last message_delta already holds the total and summing double-counts.
Ping events carry hidden usage that the dashboard should subtract.
options.why: Ping events carry no usage at all; they are keep-alive events, so subtracting anything for them changes nothing.

options.text: The API bills output tokens at one third of the streamed count because streaming is discounted.
options.why: Streaming has no pricing effect; output tokens cost the same whether streamed or not, so a discount cannot explain the gap.

options.text: The message_start event reports the final output count and later deltas should be ignored.
options.why: message_start carries only a placeholder output count and a null stop_reason; the final totals arrive in message_delta, so ignoring deltas would under-report.

question: A harness receives stop_reason "tool_use", runs the tool, then appends two messages: a user text message "Tool finished, here is the output" and a second user message with the tool_result block. The next request fails with a 400 saying tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after. What is the MOST likely fix?
explanation: The tool_result must be the first content in the user message that immediately follows the tool_use message; consecutive user messages are merged, so the text still lands in front of the result and breaks the rule.
realWorldUsage: Build the results message first, then append commentary blocks to it, never the other way around.

options.text: Put the tool_result block first in the user message that directly follows the assistant tool_use message, with any text placed after the results in that same message.
Add a system prompt line asking Claude to tolerate delayed tool results.
options.why: The ordering rule is enforced by request validation before the model runs, so no instruction to the model can make a misordered history acceptable.

options.text: Switch to Claude Opus 5, which accepts tool results in any position.
options.why: The tool_result placement rule applies to every model; changing models leaves the invalid message structure and the 400 in place.

options.text: Set is_error true on the tool_result so the API skips the ordering check.
options.why: is_error tells Claude the tool failed; it does not relax validation, and here the tool succeeded, so it would also mislead the model.

question: An agent works well for two tool calls, then starts returning empty responses (two or three tokens, stop_reason "end_turn", no content) right after tool results. The harness appends the text "Continue your analysis." after every tool_result block. What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: Appending text right after tool results trains Claude within the conversation to expect user input after each tool, producing empty end_turn responses; send tool results alone and, if needed, add a continuation prompt as a new user message only as a last resort.
realWorldUsage: Keep tool-result messages pure; put orchestration hints in the system prompt, not after every result.

options.text: Text blocks added immediately after tool results teach Claude that the user always speaks after a tool, so it ends its turn and waits.
The tool results are too long and are silently truncated by the API, leaving Claude nothing to say.
options.why: The API does not silently truncate tool results; an oversized request fails with an explicit error rather than producing empty turns.

options.text: max_tokens is too low for a response after tool use.
options.why: A max_tokens cutoff reports stop_reason max_tokens with partial content, not an empty end_turn, so the stop reason rules this out.

options.text: The model needs interleaved thinking enabled to continue after tool results.
options.why: Claude chains tool calls with or without interleaved thinking; the symptom follows the message structure, not the thinking configuration.

source.quote: Never add text blocks immediately after tool results: This teaches Claude to expect user input after every tool use.

question: A legal team sends a 900-page PDF as base64 to Claude Opus 5 (1M context) and the request is rejected for exceeding the page limit. Which change fixes this with the LEAST amount of change to the pipeline?
explanation: The page limit is 600 per request on 1M-context models, so splitting the document into chunks under that limit is the only option that addresses the rejection directly. Size chunks by tokens as well: at 1,500 to 3,000 text tokens plus image tokens per page, a dense 600-page chunk can overflow the 1M context window and fail with "prompt is too long", so far smaller chunks are usually needed in practice.
realWorldUsage: Chunk by logical sections and label each request so citations map back to the original page numbers.

options.text: Split the PDF into chunks that stay under the 600-page limit and send each chunk in its own request.
Upload the PDF to the Files API and reference it by file_id instead of base64.
options.why: The Files API shrinks the request payload, but the 600-page limit applies to the pages in the request regardless of source, so the same rejection returns.

options.text: Switch to Claude Haiku 4.5 because smaller models process documents faster.
options.why: Haiku 4.5 has a 200k context window, where the limit drops to 100 pages per request, so the change makes the problem worse.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to read every page.
options.why: max_tokens caps output; the page limit is an input validation and is unaffected by the output budget.

source.quote: A single request can include up to 600 images or PDF pages (100 for models with a 200k-token context window).

question: A browser-automation agent attaches a base64 screenshot to every turn. By turn 25 requests fail with a 413 request_too_large because the resent history exceeds 32 MB. Which change is MOST effective at keeping requests small without losing earlier screenshots?
explanation: Referencing screenshots by file_id keeps each turn's payload small no matter how many images accumulate, because the bytes are stored once instead of resent in every request.
realWorldUsage: Any agent that accumulates media in its history should adopt file_id references before it hits the request-size ceiling.

options.text: Upload each screenshot once to the Files API and reference it by file_id in the history, so payloads stop growing with every resend.
Increase JPEG compression on new screenshots.
options.why: Harder compression slows the growth but the history still resends every earlier image; it treats the symptom and degrades the legibility of on-screen text.

options.text: Move to a model with a 1M-token context window.
options.why: The 413 is a byte-size limit on the HTTP request, not a token limit; a bigger context window does not change the 32 MB cap.

options.text: Ask Claude in the system prompt to remember earlier screenshots so they can be dropped.
options.why: The API is stateless; dropped images are gone, and a prompt cannot make the model retain data that is not in the request.

source.quote: For images you'll use repeatedly or when you want to avoid encoding overhead, use the Files API. Upload the image once, then reference the returned file_id in subsequent messages instead of resending base64 data.

question: A custom streaming client rebuilds each thinking block by concatenating thinking_delta text and stores it as a thinking block with only the text. The next request in the tool-use turn fails with a 400 about thinking blocks. What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: Each streamed thinking block ends with a signature_delta before its content_block_stop; a replayed block without that signature fails verification, so accumulate the signature or use the SDK's message accumulator.
realWorldUsage: If you hand-roll SSE handling, treat signature_delta as part of the block, not an optional extra.

options.text: The client never captured the signature_delta that arrives just before content_block_stop, so the replayed block lacks the signature the API verifies.
thinking_delta text must be sent back in a text block, not a thinking block.
options.why: Thinking must be replayed as thinking blocks; converting it to text is itself a modification of the assistant message and would still fail.

options.text: Streaming responses cannot be replayed; only non-streaming responses carry valid thinking blocks.
options.why: Streamed thinking blocks are complete once accumulated with their signature; SDK accumulators produce exactly the object a non-streaming call returns.

options.text: The client should set display to omitted so no thinking text needs to be stored.
options.why: Omitted blocks still carry a signature that must be replayed; hiding the text does not remove the requirement, and this 400 comes from the missing signature, not from the text.

source.quote: For thinking content, a special signature_delta event is sent just before the content_block_stop event. This signature is used to verify the integrity of the thinking block.

question: A SaaS product on the Files API serves many customers from one Claude workspace. Each customer's browser sends the file_id of the document to analyze, and the backend forwards it straight into the Messages request. Which design is the MOST secure?
explanation: Files are visible to every API key in a workspace, so isolation comes from your own authorization layer plus one workspace per tenant, never from client-supplied file IDs.
realWorldUsage: Treat file_id like a database primary key you never expose to the browser.

options.text: Keep file IDs server-side, authorize the caller against your own user-to-file mapping, and give each tenant its own workspace with its own scoped API keys.
Keep the design but instruct Claude in the system prompt to refuse documents that do not belong to the current user.
options.why: Claude cannot tell who owns a file; the API serves any file in the workspace to any key in it, so a prompt is not an access control.

options.text: Sign each file_id with an HMAC so tampering is detectable.
options.why: Signing proves the ID was issued by you, not that the caller may read that file; it still lets the client choose the file and does nothing about workspace-wide visibility.

options.text: Delete every file immediately after each request so nothing lingers.
options.why: This treats the symptom; while a file exists any key in the workspace can read it, and re-uploading per request defeats the purpose of the Files API.

source.quote: Files are scoped to the workspace they were uploaded in.

question: An agent on Claude Opus 5 uses a single cache_control breakpoint on the last block of each request. Each turn adds roughly 25 new blocks across a dozen sequential tool round-trips. Cache reads are high during turn 2 but fall to zero from turn 3 onward, while the transcript itself never changes. Which change MOST reliably restores cache hits?
explanation: The lookback checks at most 20 positions behind a breakpoint for entries earlier requests wrote; when a turn adds more than that, a second breakpoint placed where the previous turn ended keeps a written entry inside the window.
realWorldUsage: For fan-out agents, cache at two points: the stable prefix and the end of the last completed turn.

options.text: Add a second breakpoint on the last block of the previous turn so an entry is written within the 20-position lookback window of each new breakpoint.
Switch every breakpoint to the 1-hour TTL so entries survive longer.
options.why: The entries are not expiring; they sit outside the 20-block lookback window, and TTL does not change how far back the lookback searches.

options.text: Reduce max_tokens so the assistant emits fewer blocks per turn.
options.why: Fewer output tokens do not reliably cut the number of tool_use and tool_result blocks in a dozen round-trips; it attacks the symptom indirectly and risks truncated tool calls.

options.text: Remove the breakpoint and rely on the top-level automatic cache_control.
options.why: Automatic caching also places a single breakpoint on the last block and uses the same 20-block lookback, so it misses in exactly the same way.

source.quote: The lookback window is 20 blocks. The system checks at most 20 positions per breakpoint, counting the breakpoint itself as the first.

question: A visual QA assistant keeps the full conversation in messages and, "to be safe", also re-attaches every previously sent image to each new user turn. Input tokens per turn roughly double and cost climbs. Which change is the MOST cost-effective?
explanation: Every image block in the request is billed each turn, and earlier turns already contain the originals, so re-attaching copies only duplicates visual tokens; send each image once and ask follow-up questions in text.
realWorldUsage: Distinguish bytes from tokens: file_id trims bytes, message hygiene trims tokens.

options.text: Keep each image only in the turn where it was first sent; Claude can see every image already in the history, so later questions need no copies.
Switch the copies from base64 to url sources.
options.why: A url image costs the same visual tokens as base64; it only changes payload bytes, not the duplicated tokens.

options.text: Downscale the copies to 200 px before re-attaching them.
options.why: Fewer tokens per copy, but the copies are still redundant, and images around 200 px or smaller degrade what the model can read.

options.text: Upload the images to the Files API and re-attach them by file_id.
options.why: file_id keeps requests small in bytes, but each attached image block is still tokenized on every turn, so the doubled token cost remains.

source.quote: Claude has access to every image from earlier turns, so follow-up questions such as "Are these similar to the first two?" work without including the earlier images again in the new turn's content.

question: A support bot asks for an order number, the user supplies it, and two turns later the bot asks for it again. The backend stores nothing and sends only the newest user message in each Messages API call. Which change is MOST likely to fix the problem?
explanation: The Messages API keeps no state between calls, so the client must resend the whole transcript each time; prompts, metadata and output budgets cannot substitute for the missing history.
realWorldUsage: Persist the transcript in your own store and replay it; the API will never do it for you.

options.text: Send the full conversation history, alternating user and assistant messages, in every request.
Add "Remember everything the user has told you" to the system prompt.
options.why: The API is stateless; no instruction can give the model access to earlier turns that are absent from the request.

options.text: Set metadata.user_id to the customer's ID so the API links the requests together.
options.why: user_id is an opaque identifier used for abuse detection; it does not create a session or attach prior messages.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to recall earlier context.
options.why: max_tokens caps output length; it has nothing to do with what the model was given as input.

source.quote: The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API. You can use this pattern to build up a conversation over time.

question: After a refactor, a data agent that used to request three independent lookups in one turn now requests them one at a time, tripling latency. The refactor changed the harness to send each tool_result in its own user message as soon as it is ready. What is the MOST likely explanation?
explanation: All tool_result blocks for a turn must be returned together in one user message; splitting them across messages conditions Claude to serialize its calls.
realWorldUsage: If parallel calls disappear, inspect the transcript shape before touching prompts or models.

options.text: Returning results in separate user messages teaches Claude that only one call is answered per turn, so it stops issuing parallel tool calls.
Parallel tool use was switched off server-side and must be re-enabled by setting disable_parallel_tool_use to false.
options.why: Parallel calls are on by default; the flag only exists to turn them off, and nothing in the refactor set it.

options.text: The model was downgraded and smaller models cannot call tools in parallel.
options.why: Claude 4 and later models issue parallel calls by default across tiers; the change in behavior tracks the message-structure change, not model capability.

options.text: The system prompt needs a stronger instruction such as "always batch tool calls".
options.why: Prompting can raise parallelism, but here the history contradicts the instruction on every turn; fixing the result format is the cause-level fix.

source.quote: The most common issue is formatting tool results incorrectly in the conversation history. This "teaches" Claude to avoid parallel calls.

question: A response ends with stop_reason "tool_use" and contains a server_tool_use block for web_search with no matching result block plus a client tool_use for lookup_account. Which continuation MOST reliably lets Claude finish the turn?
explanation: When client and server tools are called in the same group, reply with a user message of tool_result blocks only and an unchanged tools array; the API attaches your results, runs the deferred server tool and continues the turn.
realWorldUsage: Detect pending server calls by matching each server_tool_use id against result blocks; there is no other marker.

options.text: Send a user message containing only the tool_result for lookup_account, keep the same tools array including web_search, and let the API run the pending search on that request.
Send the tool_result followed by a text block explaining that the search is still pending.
options.why: Any content after the tool_result blocks ends the assistant turn, and the request then fails with a 400 naming the unresolved web_search tool use.

options.text: Remove web_search from tools on the follow-up so the model does not search again.
options.why: The pending server tool must still be defined; dropping it fails with a 400 whose message ends with "but no web_search tool was provided".

options.text: Resend the assistant response as-is, as you would for pause_turn.
options.why: pause_turn continuation applies when no client tool is waiting; here a client tool_use needs a result, and sending the response back without it leaves that tool_use unanswered.

source.quote: The continuation is a user message of tool_result blocks, one for every tool_use block in the response (see Handle tool calls), with two extra rules: that message must contain nothing except the tool_result blocks, and the request must keep the same tools array. A resume request that no longer defines the waiting server tool fails with a 400 whose message ends but no `web_search` tool was provided. The API attaches your results to the still-open assistant turn, runs the deferred server tool (for paused code execution, resumes it), and continues the turn.

question: On Claude Haiku 4.5 a request sets thinking type "enabled" with budget_tokens 20000 and max_tokens 16000, and it fails with a 400. What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: In manual extended thinking the budget is a subset of max_tokens, so the request must leave room for the answer: raise max_tokens above the budget or lower the budget.
realWorldUsage: Set max_tokens to the budget plus the longest answer you expect, then read thinking_tokens to tune the budget down.

options.text: budget_tokens must be less than max_tokens because thinking tokens count toward the turn's output limit.
Haiku 4.5 requires adaptive thinking, so the enabled type is rejected.
options.why: Haiku 4.5 supports extended thinking only and rejects adaptive; the enabled type is the correct one for this model.

options.text: budget_tokens must be a multiple of 1,024.
options.why: The only floor is a minimum of 1,024 tokens; there is no multiple-of rule.

options.text: max_tokens above 8,192 requires the streaming flag on Haiku 4.5.
options.why: The SDKs ask for streaming above 21,333 tokens as a client-side check; the API itself imposes no such rule, and 16,000 is below that threshold anyway.

source.quote: Thinking tokens count toward the max_tokens limit for the turn, so the budget must leave room for the final response.

question: On Claude Sonnet 4.6 a request sets thinking type "enabled" with budget_tokens 4000 and tool_choice type "any", and it fails with a 400. Which change is the MOST likely to make the request valid while keeping both reasoning and a guaranteed tool call?
explanation: Manual extended thinking only allows tool_choice auto or none; adaptive thinking lifts that restriction, so switching modes keeps reasoning and permits forced tool use.
realWorldUsage: On 4.6 and later, default to adaptive thinking so thinking and tool_choice never fight.

options.text: Switch to adaptive thinking, which supports forced tool use on this model.
Raise budget_tokens above max_tokens so the model has enough room to think before the forced call.
options.why: budget_tokens must stay below max_tokens except with interleaved thinking, so this adds a second validation error and leaves the forced-tool conflict in place.

options.text: Keep manual thinking and change tool_choice to none.
options.why: none is accepted with manual thinking but prevents any tool call, contradicting the requirement of a guaranteed call.

options.text: Add the interleaved-thinking beta header so forced tools are allowed.
options.why: The interleaved header changes where thinking appears between tool calls; it does not lift the manual-mode restriction on the any and tool choices.

source.quote: Forced tool use (tool_choice: {"type": "any"} or {"type": "tool", ...}) is incompatible with manual extended thinking but works with adaptive thinking.

question: An extraction service forces JSON output by ending messages with an assistant turn containing "{" and parsing the continuation. After moving from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to Claude Sonnet 5 every request returns a 400. Which fix requires the LEAST amount of change while keeping guaranteed JSON?
explanation: Assistant prefill is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models; structured outputs through output_config.format replace it with a schema-enforced JSON response.
realWorldUsage: Treat any trailing assistant message in your request builder as a migration blocker for current models.

options.text: Drop the prefilled assistant turn and request the schema through output_config.format so the response is schema-validated JSON.
Keep the prefill but add "}" to stop_sequences so the model closes the object.
options.why: Prefill itself returns a 400 on Claude 4.6 and later, so any request that still ends with an assistant turn fails before stop sequences matter.

options.text: Move the "{" into the last user message instead of an assistant turn.
options.why: That is just text in the prompt, not a constraint on the reply; the model may answer with prose, and nothing validates the JSON.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 so the model reliably starts with "{".
options.why: Non-default temperature is rejected on Claude 4.7 and later, and even where accepted it never guaranteed a JSON-only reply.

source.quote: JSON outputs (output_config.format): Get Claude's response in a specific JSON format, for example to extract data from images or text, generate structured reports, or format API responses.

question: A latency-sensitive assistant wants its 15k-token system prompt cached before the first user of the day arrives. Which approach is the MOST cost-effective way to warm the cache?
explanation: A max_tokens 0 request reads the prompt, writes the cache at the explicit breakpoint on the shared prefix and returns an empty response with no output tokens billed.
realWorldUsage: Fire the warm-up at deploy time and on a timer shorter than the TTL, using the same thinking and effort settings as production.

options.text: Send a request with max_tokens 0, the system prompt carrying an explicit cache_control breakpoint, and a placeholder user message.
Send a normal request with max_tokens 1 and discard the one-token reply.
options.why: It warms the cache but bills an output token and produces a reply to throw away; the zero-token form exists to replace this workaround.

options.text: Use top-level automatic cache_control with a placeholder user question.
options.why: Automatic caching puts the breakpoint on the last block, the placeholder, so the entry is keyed to text real traffic never sends and the first user request still misses.

options.text: Set the system prompt's TTL to 1 hour so it stays cached overnight.
options.why: A TTL only extends an entry that already exists and never exceeds an hour; nothing is written until a request runs.

source.quote: The max_tokens: 0 approach is preferred: no output is produced, so there is no single-token reply to discard, no output tokens are billed, and the intent of the request is unambiguous.

question: To save tokens, a pipeline extracts PDF text with a local library and sends it as a plain text block. Questions about charts and table layouts in the PDFs are answered wrong or with "no chart is present". Which change is MOST likely to fix this?
explanation: PDF support works by converting each page to an image and pairing it with extracted text, so charts are only visible when the file is sent as a document block rather than as pre-extracted text.
realWorldUsage: Pre-extract text only for text-only documents; anything with figures goes in as a document block.

options.text: Send the PDF as a document block so the API renders each page as an image alongside its extracted text.
Raise max_tokens so the model can describe the charts in more detail.
options.why: The model never received the charts; a larger output budget cannot recover information absent from the input.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window.
options.why: The input is small already; the problem is missing visual content, not window size.

options.text: Add a system prompt instruction to pay close attention to charts.
options.why: Instructions cannot make the model see pixels that were stripped out before the request was built.

source.quote: The system converts each page of the document into an image. The text from each page is extracted and provided alongside each page's image.

question: A comparison feature sends the question "Which of these two dashboards has the anomaly?" as the first content block, followed by two image blocks with no labels. Answers often refer to the wrong screenshot. Which change is MOST likely to improve accuracy at no extra cost?
explanation: Claude performs best with images before text, and labeling each image lets both the prompt and later turns refer to a specific one unambiguously.
realWorldUsage: Standardize a helper that emits "Image N:" labels ahead of every image block.

options.text: Put the images first, each preceded by a short label such as "Image 1:" and "Image 2:", and place the question after them.
Increase the resolution of both screenshots beyond 3000 px.
options.why: Images above the tier's long-edge limit are downscaled anyway, so this raises payload size without improving what the model sees or how it references each image.

options.text: Send each image in a separate request and merge the answers in code.
options.why: Splitting removes the model's ability to compare the two images jointly, which is the point of the feature, and doubles the request count.

options.text: Move the question into the system prompt.
options.why: Placement in system versus user does not label the images; the ambiguity about which image is which remains.

source.quote: When sending several images, introduce each one with a short text label (Image 1:, Image 2:, and so on) so you can refer to them by name in your prompt and in follow-up turns.

question: A team calls the token counting endpoint with a request that includes a system prompt, a client tool get_invoice, a web_search server tool, an image referenced by file_id, and a prior assistant turn containing thinking blocks. The call returns invalid_request_error. Which two parts of the request are MOST likely responsible? (Choose two.)
explanation: count_tokens rejects server tools other than the advisor tool and any image or document block with a url or file source; send images as base64 and drop server tools to count the rest.
realWorldUsage: Keep a count-only variant of your request builder that swaps file sources for base64 and strips server tools.

options.text: The web_search server tool in tools.
The client tool get_invoice.
options.why: Client tools are supported by count_tokens; their definitions are counted like any other input.

options.text: The image referenced by file_id.
The system prompt.
options.why: System prompts are counted normally; the endpoint accepts the same system field as a Messages request.

options.text: The thinking blocks in the earlier assistant turn.
options.why: count_tokens accepts thinking blocks in history and applies the model's preservation rules to them; they do not cause an error.

source.quote: This endpoint returns an invalid_request_error for a few inputs that the Messages API accepts: server tools such as web search, web fetch, code execution, and tool search (every server tool except the advisor tool), the MCP connector, and image or document blocks with a url or file source. Send images and PDFs as base64 to count them. For requests that use server tools or MCP servers, the Messages API response reports the tokens used in its usage object.

question: A team caches tools, system prompt and messages with three breakpoints and is planning several changes. Which two changes are LEAST disruptive to the cache, leaving both the tools and the system entries readable? (Choose two.)
explanation: tool_choice changes and the presence or absence of images affect only the messages level of the tools, system, messages hierarchy, while tool edits, web search toggles and system prompt edits invalidate higher levels.
realWorldUsage: Before shipping a prompt or tool tweak, classify it by hierarchy level to predict the cache rebuild cost.

options.text: Switching tool_choice from auto to any on some requests.
Rewording one tool's description.
options.why: Tool definitions are the first level of the prefix; any edit invalidates the tools, system and messages caches together.

options.text: Adding a screenshot image to the latest user message.
Enabling the web_search tool for some requests.
options.why: Toggling web search modifies the system prompt, so the system and messages caches are invalidated even though the tools entry survives.

options.text: Appending one sentence to the top-level system prompt.
options.why: Any change to the system field, even an addition, changes its hash and invalidates the system and messages caches.

source.quote: As described in Structuring your prompt, the cache follows the hierarchy: tools → system → messages. Changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels.

question: A screenshot tool must return both a caption and the captured image to Claude in one tool_result. Which two block types are the MOST appropriate to place inside the tool_result content array? (Choose two.)
explanation: tool_result content accepts text, image, document and search_result blocks, so a text caption plus an image block returns both the description and the pixels in one result.
realWorldUsage: Return screenshots as image blocks, not as base64 strings pasted into text, so Claude actually sees them.

options.text: A text block with the caption.
An image block with the screenshot as base64.
A tool_use block that re-invokes the screenshot tool.
options.why: tool_use blocks belong to assistant messages; a tool_result may hold only content blocks such as text, image, document and search_result.

options.text: A nested tool_result block for the image.
options.why: tool_result blocks cannot be nested; each result is a flat container of content blocks keyed by one tool_use_id.

options.text: A thinking block describing what the screenshot shows.
options.why: Thinking blocks are model-generated assistant content; a client cannot fabricate them, and they are not allowed inside a tool_result.

source.quote: These content blocks can use the text, image, document, or search_result types.

question: A harness on Claude Opus 5 with adaptive thinking receives a response containing thinking, tool_use and text blocks, runs the tool, and prepares the follow-up request. Which two practices MOST reliably keep the follow-up valid? (Choose two.)
explanation: Within a tool-use turn, echo the assistant content unchanged and hold the thinking and effort configuration steady; both editing blocks and toggling modes mid-turn break the turn.
realWorldUsage: Treat the assistant message as immutable and the thinking config as per-turn state that only changes between user turns.

options.text: Replay the assistant message exactly as received, including thinking and redacted_thinking blocks, before the tool_result message.
Keep the same thinking configuration and effort for the follow-up request as for the request that produced the tool_use.
Drop the thinking blocks and keep only tool_use, since the signature is stored server-side.
options.why: Nothing is stored server-side; within a tool-use turn thinking blocks are required, and their absence is a modification of the latest assistant message.

options.text: Move the thinking block after the tool_use block so the tool call comes first.
options.why: Reordering the consecutive thinking sequence counts as a modification and is rejected with a 400.

options.text: Disable thinking on the follow-up to save output tokens.
options.why: Toggling mid-turn silently disables thinking for that request, strips reasoning and invalidates the message cache; the turn's earlier thinking was already billed.

source.quote: To keep thinking valid, send every assistant turn back exactly as you received it and add new messages only at the end of messages.

question: A logistics company must classify 180,000 archived delivery-exception notes into root-cause categories to seed a new dashboard. The dashboard launch is three days away, and nobody reads an individual classification before then. Which approach is the MOST cost-effective way to run this backfill?
explanation: Route the backfill through the Message Batches API: the workload is latency-tolerant, results are needed only by the launch, and batch requests cost 50% of standard prices within a 24-hour completion window per batch. Rate limiting, caching and fast mode either leave the price unchanged or raise it.
realWorldUsage: Any job whose consumer is a scheduled process rather than a waiting human is a batch candidate by default.

options.text: Keep calling the synchronous Messages API but add a client-side rate limiter so the job never exceeds the organization's requests-per-minute limit.
options.why: A rate limiter changes when requests are sent, not what they cost; synchronous calls are billed at full price no matter how smoothly they are paced, so this treats the throttling symptom and leaves the bill untouched.

options.text: Submit the notes through the Message Batches API as two batches of at most 100,000 requests, keyed by custom_id, and collect the results before the launch.
Add a one-hour prompt-cache breakpoint to the synchronous calls so every request after the first is a cache hit.
options.why: Caching discounts only the cached prefix, and a short classification prompt has little shared prefix; the note itself and every output token are still billed at full synchronous rates. The mechanism is real but aimed at the wrong cost driver.

options.text: Enable fast mode on the synchronous calls so the job finishes in a fraction of the time and frees the workers sooner.
options.why: Fast mode is a premium-priced option that raises output speed for latency-sensitive traffic, the opposite of what a three-day backfill needs, and it cannot be combined with the batch discount at all.

source.quote: The Batches API offers significant cost savings. All usage is charged at 50% of the standard API prices.

question: A pipeline writes batch results into a table of source documents. The .jsonl results file is streamed line by line. Which is the MOST reliable way to attach each result to its source row?
explanation: Join on custom_id, the caller-chosen identifier that every result line echoes back; it is the only field designed to survive the reordering that batch processing makes no promises about.
realWorldUsage: Make custom_id your own primary key so the write-back is a single keyed update per line.

options.text: Use the line's position in the results file, since requests were submitted in table order.
options.why: Batch results can be returned in any order and frequently do not match submission order, so position-based joins silently attach outputs to the wrong documents.

options.text: Look up the source row by the custom_id echoed on each result line.
Match on the assistant message id in result.message.id, which the pipeline recorded when the batch was created.
options.why: Message ids are generated when the model produces a message, after submission, so nothing in the pipeline could have recorded them at creation time; the variable is real but unavailable when the join needs it.

options.text: Sort both the results and the source table by timestamp and zip them together.
options.why: Results carry no per-request completion timestamp you control, and concurrent processing means completion order is unrelated to source order, so sorting reconstructs nothing.

source.quote: Use meaningful custom_id values to easily match results with requests, since order is not guaranteed.

question: A payments team wants to cut LLM costs. Their fraud explainer runs during checkout and must return within two seconds, and a separate weekly chargeback summary runs on Sunday nights. Which change is the MOST appropriate use of the Message Batches API?
explanation: Use the Batches API only for the latency-tolerant Sunday summary and leave the two-second checkout path on the synchronous API; batch is a pricing tier bought with latency, not a faster or cheaper version of the same call.
realWorldUsage: Classify each call site by who waits for the answer before deciding which API serves it.

options.text: Move both workloads to the Batches API to capture the 50% discount everywhere.
options.why: The batch discount buys asynchronous processing that may take up to 24 hours; the checkout path has a two-second budget, so moving it to batch is a scope error that breaks the product to save money.

options.text: Keep the checkout explainer on the synchronous Messages API and move the Sunday chargeback summary to the Batches API.
Move the checkout explainer to the Batches API with polling every second so results arrive almost as fast.
options.why: Polling frequency does not change processing time; a batch result is available only when the request has been processed, which is best effort within 24 hours, so tight polling just adds request-rate-limit pressure.

options.text: Keep both synchronous and move the Sunday summary to off-peak hours to get lower per-token prices.
options.why: Standard API prices are per token by model, with documented modifiers for caching, batch, fast mode and data residency; the time of day is not one of them, so rescheduling changes nothing on the bill and leaves the genuinely batchable workload on the full-price API.

source.quote: This approach is well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour while reducing costs by 50% and increasing throughput.

question: A 90,000-request batch ended with 4,000 results of type expired. The engineer on call must decide what to do. Which statement is MOST correct?
explanation: Expired results mean the 24-hour window closed before those requests were processed; they are unbilled, so resubmit exactly those custom_ids in a fresh batch and keep the successes.
realWorldUsage: Log expired counts per batch so you can shrink batch size or shift submission time before it becomes a nightly problem.

options.text: The expired requests were billed and must be disputed with support before resubmission.
options.why: Expired requests never reached the model and are explicitly not billed; opening a dispute chases a charge that does not exist.

options.text: The expired requests were never sent to the model, are not billed, and should be resubmitted by custom_id in a new batch, ideally smaller or at a quieter time.
Resubmit the entire original batch, because a batch is atomic and partial results cannot be trusted.
options.why: Each request is processed independently and the 86,000 successes are complete and already paid for; resubmitting everything pays for them twice and is the brute-force answer to a per-request problem.

options.text: Wait, because expired requests are automatically retried by the service within the 29-day results window.
options.why: The 29 days is how long results stay downloadable; nothing is retried after the 24-hour processing window closes, so waiting produces no new results.

source.quote: Batch reached its 24-hour expiration before this request could be sent to the model. You will not be billed for these requests.

question: After 20 hours a batch ends and 30% of the results are errored with invalid_request_error because a new field in the request builder was misnamed. The team wants to catch this earlier next time. Which is the MOST efficient safeguard?
explanation: Dry-run a single request shape through the synchronous Messages API, where validation errors return immediately, before committing the batch; that is the documented way around batch validation being asynchronous.
realWorldUsage: Put the dry-run in the same CI step that deploys a change to the request builder.

options.text: Submit the full batch, poll every minute, and cancel as soon as the first errored result appears.
options.why: Per-request validation in a batch is asynchronous and reported only when processing of the whole batch has ended, so there is no early signal to poll for; the mechanism exists but does not fire when this plan needs it.

options.text: Before submitting, send one request built by the same code through the synchronous Messages API and fail the job if it returns a 400.
Split the job into batches of 100 so a bad build wastes at most 100 requests.
options.why: Tiny batches multiply the polling and rate-limit overhead and still only reveal the error after each batch ends; it shrinks the blast radius instead of preventing the failure.

options.text: Wrap the results loop in a catch block that discards errored results so the pipeline finishes cleanly.
options.why: Discarding errors hides the 30% of documents that were never processed and produces a report that looks complete but is not.

source.quote: Dry run a single request shape with the Messages API to avoid validation errors.

question: A weekly batch of 60,000 requests shares a 30,000-token rulebook. Cache hit rates hover near 20% because requests are processed concurrently in arbitrary order. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to raise hits?
explanation: Seed the cache with a single-request batch carrying a one-hour cache breakpoint on the shared rulebook, then release the bulk of the requests; the one-hour entry survives the minutes-to-an-hour typical batch runtime and the batch and cache discounts stack.
realWorldUsage: Wire the seed step into the pipeline as a gate that waits for processing_status ended before the bulk submit.

options.text: Move the rulebook out of the prompt and into a tool the model can call when it needs a passage.
options.why: This is a redesign of the task, not a caching fix: every request still needs the rules, and tool round-trips add output tokens and turns rather than removing the repeated input cost.

options.text: Include a request with max_tokens set to 0 at the start of the batch to pre-warm the cache.
options.why: max_tokens of 0 is rejected inside a batch because an ephemeral entry written during batch processing would likely expire before the follow-up runs; the pre-warm mechanism belongs to the synchronous API.

options.text: Mark the rulebook with a one-hour cache_control block, submit a single-request batch to write it, then submit the remaining requests once that batch has ended.
Submit the batch as 60,000 separate single-request batches so each one is processed in order.
options.why: This reverses the point of batching, hits the batch request-rate limit, and still gives no ordering guarantee across batches; processing order is the service's decision either way.

source.quote: Send a batch request with a single request that has this shared prefix and a 1-hour cache block. This writes the prefix to the 1-hour cache.

question: A vendor runs batch jobs for several customers. Results contain confidential documents, and a customer asks for assurance that no other customer's integration could read them. Which design is the MOST secure?
explanation: Isolate customers by workspace: batches, their results and uploaded files are visible to every API key in the workspace they were created in, so the workspace, not the key or the custom_id, is the boundary that gives one customer hard isolation from another.
realWorldUsage: Make "one workspace per tenant" a provisioning rule and issue tenant keys only from their own workspace.

options.text: Prefix every custom_id with the customer's identifier and filter results by prefix when downloading.
options.why: custom_id is a label for joining results, not an access control; anyone with a key in the workspace can download the whole results file regardless of prefixes.

options.text: Issue a separate API key to each customer's integration, all created in the vendor's Default Workspace.
options.why: Batches are scoped to the workspace, and any key in that workspace can view all batches and results created there, so per-customer keys change auditing but not access.

options.text: Create one workspace per customer and run each customer's batches with keys issued from that workspace.
Delete each batch immediately after downloading its results and rely on the deletion for isolation.
options.why: Deletion shortens the exposure window, but the results are readable by every key in the workspace from the moment the batch ends until the delete runs; it mitigates after the fact rather than preventing access.

source.quote: You may view all batches (and their results) that were created within the Workspace your request runs in.

question: A visual inspection agent receives a 6 MB photo on turn one and then exchanges 40 tool-use turns about it. Every request now carries the photo again and p95 latency has doubled. Which change is the MOST efficient fix that keeps the photo in the model's context?
explanation: Upload the image once to the Files API and reference the returned file_id in later turns; the conversation history then carries a small reference instead of 6 MB of base64 on every request, while the model still sees the full image.
realWorldUsage: Adopt file_id references whenever an image or PDF will outlive the request that introduced it.

options.text: Drop the image from the history after turn one and describe it in text instead.
options.why: This changes what the model can see: later questions about details in the photo can no longer be answered from the pixels, so the fix trades correctness for payload size.

options.text: Upload the photo once with the Files API and reference its file_id in the image block on every turn.
Host the photo on a public URL and switch the image block to a url source.
options.why: A url source requires making inspection data publicly reachable, which is unacceptable for confidential photos, and it moves the bytes into a hosting problem instead of removing the repetition from the conversation.

options.text: Downscale the photo to 500 pixels and keep embedding it as base64.
options.why: Downscaling shrinks the payload but discards the detail an inspection task depends on, and the bytes are still resent on all 40 turns; it treats the symptom instead of the repetition.

source.quote: For images you'll use repeatedly or when you want to avoid encoding overhead, use the Files API. Upload the image once, then reference the returned file_id in subsequent messages instead of resending base64 data.

question: Policy requires that customer PDFs uploaded to the Files API disappear from Anthropic storage within 14 days. Which implementation has the LEAST operational overhead?
explanation: Set expires_in_seconds on each upload (14 days is 1,209,600 seconds, inside the allowed 3,600 to 7,776,000 range) so files expire automatically, and filter listings by expires_at; no cleanup job is needed.
realWorldUsage: Default your upload helper to the policy lifetime so no caller can forget it.

options.text: Run a nightly job that lists every file, compares created_at with today, and deletes anything older than 14 days.
options.why: This works but adds a scheduled process, pagination handling and failure alerting to maintain, when the API can enforce the same lifetime on each file without any job.

options.text: Pass expires_in_seconds set to 1209600 on every upload so each file expires on its own.
Request a zero data retention arrangement so uploaded files are never stored.
options.why: The Files API is not eligible for zero data retention; it stores files by definition, so ZDR is the wrong mechanism for this feature.

options.text: Re-send each PDF as base64 on every request instead of using the Files API, so nothing persists.
options.why: Resending base64 abandons the create-once benefit and inflates every payload; it removes the feature instead of configuring its lifetime.

source.quote: To have a file expire automatically, include an expires_in_seconds form field when you upload it. The value is an integer number of seconds between 3,600 (1 hour) and 7,776,000 (90 days). The resulting expires_at timestamp (RFC 3339) appears on every file response and is null for files uploaded without an expiration.

question: A team migrates a working Claude API integration to Claude in Amazon Bedrock without changing application logic. Which TWO parts of the integration are MOST likely to stop working because the platform does not offer them? (Choose two.)
explanation: Bedrock does not offer the Message Batches endpoint or the Files API (nor URL sources), so the batch job and the file_id references break; prompt caching, client-side tool use and thinking are all supported and survive the move.
realWorldUsage: Before a platform move, diff your code against the Features overview availability column rather than against the Bedrock model list.

options.text: The nightly job that submits requests to the Message Batches API.
The prompt-caching breakpoints in the system prompt.
options.why: Prompt caching, including the one-hour duration, is supported on Amazon Bedrock; the cache_control blocks keep working.

options.text: The document blocks that reference product manuals by Files API file_id.
The client-side tools defined with input_schema and answered with tool_result blocks.
options.why: Tool use with client-side tools is supported on Bedrock; only server-side tools such as web search and code execution are missing.

options.text: The adaptive thinking configuration on requests.
options.why: Thinking, including adaptive thinking on 4.6-and-later models, is available on Bedrock, so this configuration carries over unchanged.

question: A developer ports raw HTTP calls from api.anthropic.com to Google Cloud's Agent Platform by changing the base URL and the Authorization header. The body still contains "model": "claude-opus-5" and the request sends an anthropic-version header. Requests fail. What is the MOST likely cause?
explanation: Agent Platform differs from the Claude API in exactly two request-format ways: the model ID is part of the URL path (.../models/claude-opus-5:rawPredict) and anthropic_version is a body field fixed at vertex-2023-10-16; leaving the model in the body and the version in a header breaks both.
realWorldUsage: Keep platform adapters in one module so the two Google Cloud rewrites live in a single place.

options.text: Google Cloud requires a dated model ID such as claude-opus-5@20260101 in the body.
options.why: For 4.6-and-later models the Google Cloud ID matches the Claude API form, and in any case the model does not go in the body on this platform; the variable is real but the placement is the actual error.

options.text: On Agent Platform the model belongs in the endpoint URL, not the body, and anthropic_version must be sent in the body as vertex-2023-10-16 rather than as a header.
Agent Platform only accepts requests through the AnthropicVertex SDK client, never raw HTTP.
options.why: Raw HTTP works and is documented with curl; the SDK is a convenience that applies the URL and body rewrites for you, not a requirement.

options.text: The 30 MB payload limit is being exceeded because the header is counted toward it.
options.why: A short message is nowhere near 30 MB, and headers do not count toward the payload limit; this blames a limit that is not in play.

source.quote: On Agent Platform, anthropic_version is passed in the request body (rather than as a header), and must be set to the value vertex-2023-10-16.

question: An application configured for Claude in Microsoft Foundry sends "model": "claude-sonnet-5" and receives "Deployment not found", although the admin confirms Sonnet 5 is deployed in the resource. What is the MOST likely fix?
explanation: On Foundry the model parameter carries the deployment name; if the admin created the deployment under a custom name, that name, not claude-sonnet-5, is what the request must send.
realWorldUsage: Read the Target URI and deployment name from the deployment's Details tab and put both in environment config.

options.text: Switch the model string to the Bedrock-style identifier anthropic.claude-sonnet-5.
options.why: The anthropic. prefix is the Amazon Bedrock format; Foundry never uses it, so this swaps one wrong name for another.

options.text: Send the deployment name the admin chose in the Foundry portal, because on Foundry the model parameter is the deployment name, which only defaults to the model ID.
Add the anthropic-version header, which Foundry requires to resolve model IDs.
options.why: The error names a missing deployment, not a missing header; version headers do not map names to deployments.

options.text: Move the deployment to a Hosted on Anthropic version, since Hosted on Azure deployments cannot be addressed by name.
options.why: Both hosting options are addressed by deployment name in exactly the same way; hosting affects feature availability, not name resolution.

source.quote: Solution: The model parameter should contain your deployment name, which can be customized in the Foundry portal.

question: A Foundry deployment hosted on Azure returns 400 Bad Request whenever a request includes the code execution tool, while identical requests without the tool succeed. Which is the MOST direct fix?
explanation: Code execution, along with the Files API, Agent Skills, programmatic tool calling and newer web tool versions, is unavailable on deployments hosted on Azure and available on deployments hosted on Anthropic, so deploy the model's Hosted on Anthropic version and switch the deployment name.
realWorldUsage: Keep a Hosted on Anthropic deployment in the same resource for tool-heavy workloads so the endpoint and credentials stay unchanged.

options.text: Add retry with exponential backoff, since 400s on Foundry are transient capacity errors.
options.why: The 400 is by design for features unsupported on Azure-hosted deployments; retrying a deterministic rejection just repeats it.

options.text: Switch to a larger Opus deployment on the same Hosted on Azure option.
options.why: The limitation belongs to the hosting option, not the model tier; every Azure-hosted deployment rejects code execution regardless of model.

options.text: Create a Hosted on Anthropic deployment of the model and point the application at that deployment name.
Move the workload off Foundry to the Claude API, since Foundry does not support server-side tools.
options.why: Foundry does support code execution on deployments hosted on Anthropic; abandoning the platform is a bigger change than the documented one-deployment fix.

source.quote: Create a new deployment of the model's other hosting version (Hosted on Azure or Hosted on Anthropic).

question: A public-sector contractor on AWS must show FedRAMP High authorization and that AWS, not Anthropic, is the sole processor of inference data. Which TWO facts make Claude in Amazon Bedrock the MOST appropriate offering over Claude Platform on AWS? (Choose two.)
explanation: Bedrock is AWS-operated end to end, with AWS as the inference data processor, and is the documented path for FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 and HIPAA-ready needs; Claude Platform on AWS is Anthropic-operated and wins on feature parity, not on compliance posture.
realWorldUsage: Let the compliance requirement pick the operator first, then check whether the feature gaps are acceptable.

options.text: Bedrock runs entirely on AWS-controlled infrastructure with AWS as the operating party and inference data processor.
Bedrock passes anthropic-beta headers through so new features arrive the same day as on the Claude API.
options.why: That describes Claude Platform on AWS; Bedrock does not accept the anthropic-beta header and follows the Bedrock release schedule.

options.text: Bedrock is the documented choice for FedRAMP High, IL4, IL5 and HIPAA-ready requirements.
Bedrock offers the Message Batches API and Agent Skills for the contractor's overnight jobs.
options.why: Neither Batches nor Agent Skills is available on Bedrock; both are offered by Claude Platform on AWS, so this reverses the feature comparison.

options.text: Bedrock bills usage through AWS Marketplace in Claude Consumption Units.
options.why: Marketplace billing in consumption units is how Claude Platform on AWS is billed; Bedrock is billed as native AWS service usage.

source.quote: Bedrock runs entirely on AWS-controlled infrastructure with AWS as the operating party.

question: A team on Claude in Amazon Bedrock has no data-residency requirement and wants maximum availability for Sonnet 5 traffic. Which endpoint choice is MOST cost-effective?
explanation: Use the global endpoint: it gives dynamic routing across all available regions for availability at no premium, whereas regional endpoints exist for data residency and cost 10% more.
realWorldUsage: Reserve regional endpoints for workloads with a written residency requirement and let everything else ride the global endpoint.

options.text: A regional endpoint in us-east-1, because a single region has the lowest network cost.
options.why: Regional endpoints resolve to one region for data residency and carry a 10% pricing premium over global; the network-cost reasoning is not how Bedrock prices Claude.

options.text: The global endpoint, which routes dynamically across available regions with no pricing premium.
An inference profile that routes across the EU regions, since geography-scoped routing is always cheaper.
options.why: Geography-scoped inference profiles exist to keep traffic inside a region group for residency; the team has no residency need, and only the global endpoint is documented as carrying no premium.

options.text: A regional endpoint in every region with client-side round robin to spread the load.
options.why: This rebuilds the global endpoint's routing by hand while paying the 10% regional premium in each region, adding cost and code for no benefit.

source.quote: Global: dynamic routing across all available regions for maximum availability. No pricing premium.

question: A change-control board refuses to approve claude-opus-5 in production because "an ID without a date must be an alias that Anthropic can update at any time". Which response is MOST accurate?
explanation: For Claude 4.6 and later the dateless ID is the canonical pinned snapshot, never an evergreen pointer; Anthropic does not change the weights behind an existing ID and releases updates under new IDs, so claude-opus-5 is as pinned as any dated ID ever was.
realWorldUsage: Cite the Model IDs and versioning page in change-control tickets so the pinning argument does not have to be re-litigated per release.

options.text: Agree, and switch to a dated ID such as claude-opus-5-20260601 to pin the snapshot.
options.why: No dated form exists for 4.6-and-later models; inventing one produces a request for a model that does not exist.

options.text: Explain that from the 4.6 generation onward the dateless ID is itself the pinned snapshot, that improvements ship under a new ID, and that only serving infrastructure changes can cause minor behavior differences.
Agree, and add a system-prompt instruction asking the model to behave exactly as it did on the approval date.
options.why: A prompt cannot freeze weights or configuration; it is a request, not a pin, and the concern it addresses does not apply to a snapshot ID anyway.

options.text: Explain that the alias concern is valid but irrelevant because Bedrock and Google Cloud IDs are the ones that float.
options.why: Partner-platform IDs for 4.6-and-later models are pinned just as the Claude API IDs are; the floating behavior belongs only to the Claude API's pre-4.6 convenience aliases such as claude-sonnet-4-5.

source.quote: For the 4.6 generation and later, the dateless ID is the canonical model ID for that release. It maps to a single, fixed model snapshot. Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing model ID.

question: A deprecation notice gives a retirement date for the dated model ID behind three production services. Which TWO actions form the MOST reliable migration plan? (Choose two.)
explanation: Locate every caller with the Usage export and validate the recommended replacement on your own evals before the date; aliases do not migrate you, retired models fail, and dates are not negotiated per customer.
realWorldUsage: Track retirement dates for every model ID in your config repository and open the migration ticket when the notice lands.

options.text: Export the Console Usage report to CSV to find every API key and service still calling the deprecated ID.
Switch each service to the short alias for that model family so it follows the latest snapshot automatically.
options.why: The alias resolves only to dated snapshots of the same minor version, which is the one being retired; it does not hop to the recommended replacement, and it surrenders control over when behavior changes.

options.text: Run the recommended replacement model against each service's eval set well before the retirement date and fix prompts where results regress.
Keep the current ID past the retirement date, since retired models keep serving at reduced reliability.
options.why: Requests to a retired model fail outright; reduced reliability describes deprecated models before retirement, not retired ones.

options.text: Open a support request to have the retirement date extended for your organization.
options.why: Retirement dates are set per model ID with at least 60 days' notice; the documented path is migration, and support helps with migration questions rather than moving the date.

source.quote: Review the downloaded CSV to see usage broken down by API key and model.

question: A team's committed .claude/settings.json sets "model": "claude-sonnet-5". One developer wants Opus for their own sessions in this repository only, without affecting teammates or other projects. Which approach needs the LEAST amount of change?
explanation: Put the override in .claude/settings.local.json: project local settings sit above the committed project file, apply only to this developer in this project, and Claude Code keeps the file out of git.
realWorldUsage: Test new values in settings.local.json first and promote them to the shared file only when the team agrees.

options.text: Change model in the committed .claude/settings.json and ask teammates to ignore the diff.
options.why: Shared project settings apply to everyone who clones the repository, so this changes every teammate's default and creates a commit nobody else wants.

options.text: Set model in ~/.claude/settings.json.
options.why: User settings sit below shared project settings in precedence, so the project's Sonnet value still wins, and the user file would affect every other project too.

options.text: Add "model": "claude-opus-5" to .claude/settings.local.json in the repository.
Export ANTHROPIC_MODEL in the developer's shell profile.
options.why: The variable overrides model from any file, but it applies to every project the developer opens from that shell, not just this repository.

source.quote: Project local settings (.claude/settings.local.json): your personal settings for this project.
